name: 2 Samuel
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where 2 Samuel is called 2 Kingdoms) and against the Dead Sea Scrolls of Samuel, chiefly 4QSam-a, the largest of them. In Samuel the traditional Hebrew text has suffered more copying damage than in most books, and the Septuagint and 4QSam-a often preserve an older or fuller wording; the most important differences are footnoted (for example, in David’s lament for Saul and Jonathan, the list of David’s mighty men, and the census account). Every Septuagint reading cited in the footnotes was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation (quoted in modernized wording). Readings of the Dead Sea Scrolls are stated in general terms (“is reported to read”) until they can be checked against the critical editions. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (18:33; 19:1–43), a footnote says so. Measurements are given in modern US units, and times and dates use modern equivalents, with the originals in the footnotes.

verses.text: Now it came about after the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, that David remained two days in Ziklag.
On the third day, look, a man came out of the camp from Saul, with his garments torn and earth upon his head. And as he came to David, he fell to the ground and did obeisance.
David said to him, “From where do you come?” He said to him, “Out of the camp of Israel I have escaped.”

David said to him, “How did the matter go? Tell me, I pray.” He answered, “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people also have fallen and are dead; and Saul and Jonathan his son are dead too.”
Then David said to the young man who was telling him, “How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?”

The young man who brought him the report said, “I chanced to come upon Mount Gilboa, and look, Saul was propped upon his spear, and look, the chariots and the masters of horse were following hard upon him.
When he looked behind him, he saw me and called to me. And I answered, ‘Here am I.’
He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
He said to me, ‘Stand over me, I pray, and kill me, for dizziness{a} has seized me, though my life is still whole in me.’

So I stood over him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.”
Then David seized his clothes and rent them; likewise every man that was with him.
They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of Yahweh{b} and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young man who told him, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite.”
David said to him, “How were you not afraid to put forth your hand to destroy Yahweh’s anointed?”
Then David called one of the young men and said, “Go near and fall upon him.” And he struck him so that he died.
David said to him, “Your blood be upon your own head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have killed Yahweh’s anointed.’”
Then David lamented with this lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son,
and he said it should be taught to the sons of Judah: the Bow.{c} Look, it is written in the Book of Jashar.{d}
“Your glory,{e} O Israel, is slain upon your high places! How are the mighty fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath; do not announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.
You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew nor rain upon you, nor fields of offerings!{f} For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil.{g}
From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty.
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In their lives and in their death they were not divided. They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions.
You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet with delights, who put ornaments of gold upon your apparel.
How are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle! Jonathan lies slain upon your high places.
I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me. Your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.
How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!”

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain; perhaps “cramp” or “agony.” The Septuagint reads “a dreadful darkness” (Brenton).
The Septuagint reads “for the people of Judah” (reported).
The Hebrew is uncertain. “The Bow” may be the title of the lament (see verse 22). The Septuagint lacks the word (Brenton, “he gave orders to teach it the sons of Judah”).
Jashar means “upright.” The Book of Jashar was an ancient collection of poems, now lost (see also Joshua 10:13). The Septuagint reads “the book of Right” (Brenton).
Or “The gazelle.” The Hebrew word tsevi can mean either “beauty” or “gazelle.”
The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “nor fields of first-fruits” (Brenton).

Leather shields were rubbed with oil before battle. The Septuagint likewise reads “the shield of Saul was not anointed with oil” (Brenton). Some read the phrase as referring to Saul himself, “no longer anointed” (scholarly review).

verses.text: After this David inquired of Yahweh, saying, “Shall I go up into any of the towns of Judah?” Yahweh said to him, “Go up.” David said, “To where shall I go up?” And he said, “To Hebron.”{a}
So David went up there, and his two wives as well, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, who had been the wife of Nabal of Carmel.
And David brought up his men who were with him, every man with his household, and they settled in the towns of Hebron.
Then the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. They told David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.”
So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, “Blessed be you of Yahweh, because you have shown this kindness to your lord, to Saul, and have buried him.
Now may Yahweh show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I also will do you good, because you have done this thing.
So now strengthen your hands and be sons of valor; for Saul your master is dead, and me the house of Judah has anointed as king over them.”
But Abner son of Ner, captain of Saul’s army, had taken Ish-bosheth{b} son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim,{c}
and he made him king over Gilead and over the Ashurites{d} and over Jezreel and over Ephraim and over Benjamin and over all Israel.
Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
The number of the days that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
And Joab{e} son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them by the pool of Gibeon. They sat down, the one band on the one side of the pool and the other on the other side of the pool.
Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men arise now and contend before us.” Joab said, “Let them arise.”
Then they arose and went over by number, twelve for Benjamin and for Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.
Each man caught his fellow by the head and thrust his sword into his fellow’s side, and they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim,{f} which is in Gibeon.
And the fighting grew exceedingly hard that day, and Abner was beaten, and the men of Israel with him, before David’s servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab and Abishai and Asahel.{g} Asahel was as light of foot as one of the gazelles in the field.
Asahel pursued after Abner, and in going he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.
Then Abner looked behind him and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is I.”
Abner said to him, “Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and lay hold of one of the young men and take his gear for yourself.” But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.
Abner said again to Asahel, “Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to Joab your brother?”

Yet he refused to turn aside. So Abner smote him in the belly with the hinder end of the spear, and the spear went out behind him; and he fell there and died in his place. And every one who came to the spot where Asahel fell and died halted.
But Joab and Abishai chased after Abner. And the sun went down as they reached the hill of Ammah, that lies before Giah by the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The sons of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one band, and they stood on the top of a hill.

Then Abner called to Joab, “Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitterness in the end? How long will it be, then, before you bid the people turn back from following their brothers?”
Joab said, “As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the people would have gone away in the morning, each from following his brother.”{h}
So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people stood still and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight any more.
Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan and went through all the Bithron{i} and came to Mahanaim.
Joab returned from following Abner. When he had gathered all the people together, there were missing of David’s servants nineteen men, besides Asahel.
But the servants of David had struck of Benjamin and of Abner’s men three hundred and sixty men, and they died.
They took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was in Bethlehem. And Joab and his men went all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.

notes.text: Hebron was the chief city of Judah, about 19 miles (31 kilometers) south of Jerusalem. Its name perhaps means “association” or “alliance.”

Ish-bosheth means “man of shame.” His original name was Ishbaal or Eshbaal, “man of the lord” (1 Chronicles 8:33); scribes replaced “baal” with “bosheth” (“shame”) to avoid the name of the god Baal. The Septuagint reads “Jebosthe” (Brenton). Likewise throughout.
Mahanaim means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2), a town east of the Jordan.
So the Hebrew. Some ancient versions read “Geshurites” (reported); others suggest “Asherites.”
Joab means “Yahweh is father.”
Helkath-hazzurim means “field of flints” or “field of blades” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “Portion of the Treacherous ones” (reported).
Asahel means “God has made.”
Or “If you had not spoken, the people would have given up the pursuit of their brothers only in the morning.” The Hebrew can be read either way.
Or “the whole morning”; the Hebrew word bitron may be a place name or mean “ravine.”

verses.text: Now the war between Saul’s house and David’s house was long. And David went on growing ever stronger, but the house of Saul went on growing ever weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon,{a} by Ahinoam the Jezreelitess;
his second, Chileab,{b} whose mother was Abigail, formerly wife of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom{c} son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
the fourth, Adonijah{d} the son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah{e} the son of Abital;
and the sixth, Ithream,{f} by Eglah, David’s wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.
Now Saul had had a concubine whose name was Rizpah,{g} the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth{h} said to Abner, “Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?”

Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, “Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah? To this day I keep showing loyalty to the household of your father Saul, to his kinsmen and to his companions, and I have not handed you over into David’s hand; and yet you charge me today with a fault concerning this woman!
So may God do to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what Yahweh has sworn to him,
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.
Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf,{i} saying, “Whose is the land? Make your covenant with me, and look, my hand shall be with you to bring all Israel over to you.”
He said, “Good. I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you: you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, when you come to see my face.”
Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, saying, “Give me my wife Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”
So Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband, from Paltiel the son of Laish.
But her husband went with her, weeping as he went behind her as far as Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, “Go, return.” And he returned.
Now Abner had held counsel with Israel’s elders, saying, “Both yesterday and the day before you were seeking to have David as king over you.
Now then do it. For Yahweh has spoken of David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke in the ears of Benjamin. And Abner went to speak in the ears of David at Hebron all that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin.
When Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.

Abner said to David, “Let me arise and go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your soul desires.” So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
Just then the servants of David and Joab came from a raid and brought much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David in Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
When Joab and all the army that was with him came, they told Joab, “Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has sent him away, and he has gone in peace.”
Then Joab came to the king and said, “What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, and he is quite gone?
You know Abner the son of Ner, that he came to deceive you, and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing.”
When Joab had gone out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, and they turned him back from the well of Sirah;{j} and David knew nothing of it.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him quietly, and there he smote him in the stomach, and he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, “I and my kingdom are guiltless before Yahweh forever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner.

May it whirl{k} upon the head of Joab and upon all his father’s house. And may there never be lacking from the house of Joab one who has a discharge, or one who is leprous,{l} or one who leans on a staff,{m} or one who falls by the sword, or one who lacks bread!”
So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death at Gibeon in the battle.
Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, “Tear your clothes, and gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” And King David followed the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.
Then the king chanted a lament over Abner, and said, “Was Abner to die the death of a fool?
Your hands were not bound, nor your feet put into fetters. As one falls before the sons of wickedness, so you fell.” And all the people wept over him again.
Then all the people came to cause David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David took an oath: “God do so to me, and more as well, if I taste bread or anything else before sunset!”
All the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people.
So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been from the king to put to death Abner the son of Ner.
And the king spoke to his servants: “Know you not that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?
I am weak today, though anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. May Yahweh repay the evildoer according to his evil!”{n}

notes.text: Amnon means “faithful.”
Called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1. The meaning of Chileab is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “Dalouia” (reported).
Absalom means “my father is peace.” Maacah means “oppression” (uncertain); Talmai perhaps means “furrowed” (uncertain). Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
Adonijah means “my lord is Yahweh.” Haggith means “festal.”
Shephatiah means “Yahweh has judged.” The meaning of Abital is “my father is dew” (uncertain).
Ithream means “remainder of the people” (uncertain). The meaning of Eglah is “heifer.”
Rizpah means “glowing coal.” Aiah means “falcon.”
So some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint (Brenton, “Jebosthe the son of Saul”). The traditional Hebrew text lacks the name here.
Or “where he was.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Sirah means “thorn” (uncertain).
Or “fall.”
The Hebrew word covered various skin diseases.
Or “who holds a spindle,” that is, one who is unfit for war (uncertain).
The Septuagint reads “I am this day a mere kinsman of his, and as it were a subject” (Brenton, modernized). The Hebrew is difficult.

verses.text: When Saul’s son{a} heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew feeble, and all Israel was troubled.

Now Saul’s son had two men who were captains of raiding bands. The name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab,{b} sons of Rimmon a man of Beeroth, of the sons of Benjamin (for Beeroth also is reckoned to Benjamin;
the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there until this day).

Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled. And as she made haste to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.{c}
Then Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, went off, and in the heat of the day they reached the house of Ish-bosheth, while he was lying down for his midday rest.
They came there into the middle of the house as though to fetch wheat, and they struck him in the belly. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.{d}
When they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedchamber, they struck him and killed him and beheaded him. They took his head and went by the way of the Arabah all night.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul your enemy, who sought your life. Yahweh has given my lord the king vengeance this day on Saul and on his offspring.”
But David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, “As Yahweh lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,
when one told me, ‘Look, Saul is dead,’ and in his own eyes he was a bearer of good tidings, I seized him and slew him at Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news.
How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now require his blood at your hand and take you away from the earth?”

And David commanded his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and their feet and hanged them up by the pool in Hebron. But the head of Ish-bosheth they took and laid in Abner’s grave in Hebron.

notes.text: The Hebrew lacks the name here; the Septuagint reads “Memphibosthe” (reported), but most interpreters understand Ish-bosheth.
Baanah means “son of affliction” (uncertain). Rechab means “rider.” Rimmon means “pomegranate.” Beeroth means “wells.”
Mephibosheth means “from the mouth of shame.” He is called Merib-baal (“Baal contends” or “the lord is advocate”) in 1 Chronicles 8:34; see the note on Ish-bosheth at 2:8.

The Septuagint reads differently: “And behold, the porter of the house was winnowing wheat, and she slumbered and slept, and the brothers Rechab and Baanah slipped into the house” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and spoke, saying, “See, we are your bone and your flesh.

Even in time past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led Israel out and brought Israel in. And Yahweh said to you, ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.’”
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David cut a covenant with them in Hebron before Yahweh, and they anointed David king over Israel.
Thirty years old was David at his becoming king, and forty years he reigned.
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

The king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land. They said to David, “You shall not come in here; even the blind and the lame will turn you back,” thinking, “David cannot come in here.”
Nevertheless David captured the stronghold of Zion,{a} which is the City of David.

David said on that day, “Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him reach through the water shaft{b} to the lame and the blind, who are hated by David’s soul.” Therefore they say, “The blind and the lame shall not come into the house.”
David dwelt in the stronghold and called it the City of David. And David built round about from the Millo{c} inward.
And David went on and grew great, for Yahweh God of Armies was with him.
Hiram{d} king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, and carpenters and masons,{e} and they built David a house.
And David perceived that Yahweh had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
David took more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
These are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,{f}
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.{g}
When the Philistines heard that they had anointed David king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David. David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.
Now the Philistines had come and spread themselves out in the Valley of Rephaim.{h}
And David inquired of Yahweh, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?” Yahweh said to David, “Go up, for I will surely give the Philistines into your hand.”

So David came to Baal-perazim, and David struck them there. And he said, “Yahweh has broken through my enemies before me, like a breaking through of waters.” Therefore he called the name of that place Baal-perazim.{i}
They abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.{j}
Yet again the Philistines came up and spread themselves out in the Valley of Rephaim.
When David inquired of Yahweh, he said, “You shall not go up. Circle around behind them, and come upon them opposite the balsam trees.{k}
And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then bestir yourself, for then Yahweh has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.”
And David did so, as Yahweh had commanded him, and struck the Philistines from Geba{l} all the way to Gezer.

notes.text: Zion was the fortified hill of the Jebusite city, the southeastern ridge of Jerusalem. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
The Hebrew word tsinnor is uncertain; perhaps “water shaft” or “channel,” or a kind of hook or weapon (scholarly review). The Septuagint reads “let him attack with the dagger” (Brenton, modernized).
Millo means “filling,” probably a terraced earthwork.
Hiram means “my brother is exalted” (uncertain).
Hebrew “craftsmen of wood and craftsmen of stone for walls.”
Shammua means “heard.” Shobab perhaps means “returning” (uncertain). Nathan means “he has given.” Solomon is related to the word for “peace.”

Ibhar means “he chooses.” Elishua means “God is salvation.” Nepheg perhaps means “sprout” (uncertain). Japhia means “he shines forth.” Elishama means “God has heard.” Eliada means “God knows.” Eliphelet means “God is deliverance.”
Rephaim means “ghosts” or the name of an ancient people of great stature; the valley lay southwest of Jerusalem.
Baal-perazim means “lord of breaking through.”
First Chronicles 14:12 adds that they were burned.
Or “baka shrubs”; the exact kind of tree is uncertain. Likewise in verse 24.
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 14:16 read “Gibeon” (reported).

verses.text: David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.

And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah,{a} to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name, the name of Yahweh of Armies, who sits enthroned on the cherubim.
They placed the ark of God upon a new wagon and brought it out from Abinadab’s house on the hill; and Uzzah and Ahio,{b} Abinadab’s sons, drove the new wagon,
with the ark of God;{c} and Ahio went before the ark.
David and all the house of Israel were making merry before Yahweh with all kinds of instruments of fir wood,{d} with lyres and harps and tambourines and rattles and cymbals.
When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon,{e} Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, because the oxen stumbled.
And the anger of Yahweh was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him there for his error,{f} and he died there beside the ark of God.
David was angry because Yahweh had broken out against Uzzah. And he called that place Perez-uzzah,{g} as it is named to this day.
David was afraid of Yahweh that day, and he said, “How can the ark of Yahweh come to me?”
So David would not take the ark of Yahweh to himself into the City of David, but David turned it aside to the house of Obed-edom{h} the Gittite.
The ark of Yahweh remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and Yahweh blessed Obed-edom and all his household.

It was told King David, “Yahweh has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him because of the ark of God.” So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the City of David with rejoicing.
When those who carried the ark of Yahweh had gone six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.
And David danced before Yahweh with all his might, and David was girded with a linen ephod.
So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of Yahweh with shouting and with the sound of the horn.
As the ark of Yahweh came into the City of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window and saw King David leaping and whirling before Yahweh, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of Yahweh and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before Yahweh.
When David had made an end of offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of Yahweh of Armies.

And he apportioned to all the people, to the whole throng of Israel, to man and to woman, one loaf of bread apiece, a cake of dates,{i} and a cake of raisins. Then all the people departed, each to his house.

David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, “How glorious was the king of Israel today, who uncovered himself today in the eyes of his servants’ maids, as one of the empty fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!”
David said to Michal, “It was before Yahweh, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of Yahweh, over Israel; and I will make merry before Yahweh.
I will make myself yet more lightly esteemed than this, and I will be lowly in my own eyes.{j} But with the maids you speak of, with them I shall have honor.”
And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.

notes.text: Baale-judah means “lords of Judah,” another name for Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 13:6; Joshua 15:9). Some Hebrew manuscripts and other witnesses reportedly read “Baalah of Judah.”
Uzzah means “strength.” Ahio means “his brother” (uncertain); the Septuagint reads “his brothers” (reported).
The Hebrew repeats part of verse 3 here: “and they carried it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill, with the ark of God.” The Septuagint has a shorter text (reported).

So the traditional Hebrew text, literally “with all woods of cypress.” The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 13:8 read “with all their might and with songs” (Brenton, “on well-tuned instruments mightily, and with songs,” modernized).
Nacon means “prepared” (uncertain). First Chronicles 13:9 reads “Chidon.” The Septuagint reads “Nachor” (Brenton).
The Hebrew word is uncertain. First Chronicles 13:10 reads “because he put out his hand to the ark.”
Perez-uzzah means “breaking out against Uzzah.”
Obed-edom means “servant of Edom” (uncertain).
The Hebrew word is uncertain; perhaps “a portion of meat.” The Septuagint reads “a joint of meat” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “in your eyes” (reported).

verses.text: Now it came to pass, when the king lived in his house and Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies round about,
that the king said to Nathan the prophet, “See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells within curtains.”
And Nathan said to the king, “Go, do all that is in your heart, for Yahweh is with you.”
But that same night the word of Yahweh came to Nathan, saying,
“Go and tell my servant David, ‘Thus says Yahweh: Would you build me a house for me to dwell in?
For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought the sons of Israel up out of Egypt even until this day, but I have gone about in a tent and in a tabernacle.

In all places where I have walked with all the sons of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the tribes{a} of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”’
Now then, speak thus to my servant David: ‘So says Yahweh of Armies: From the sheepfold I took you, from behind the flock, that you should be prince over my people, over Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from your presence. And I will make you a great name, like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.

And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be troubled no more. And the sons of wickedness shall afflict them no more, as at the first,
from the day that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, Yahweh declares to you that Yahweh will make you a house.{b}
When your days are complete and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will make his kingdom firm.
He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he does wrong, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of Adam,
but my steadfast love shall not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you.
And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before you.{c} Your throne shall stand firm forever.’”
According to all these words and according to all this vision, so Nathan spoke to David.
Then King David went in and sat before Yahweh and said, “Who am I, Lord Yahweh, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?
And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, Lord Yahweh. You have spoken also of your servant’s house for a great while to come, and this is the instruction for mankind,{d} Lord Yahweh!
And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, Lord Yahweh!
Because of your word, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, to make your servant know it.
Therefore you are great, Lord Yahweh. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

And what one nation on the earth is like your people, like Israel, whom God went to redeem for himself as a people, and to make himself a name, and to do great and awesome things for them,{e} by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, nations and their gods?
And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, Yahweh, became their God.
And now, Yahweh God, the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, confirm it forever, and do as you have spoken.
And may your name be magnified forever, saying, ‘Yahweh of Armies is God over Israel,’ and the house of your servant David shall be established before you.
For you, Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, have revealed to your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found courage{f} to pray this prayer to you.
And now, Lord Yahweh, you are God, and your words are truth, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.

Now therefore let it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you. For you, Lord Yahweh, have spoken it, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever.”

notes.text: So the Hebrew, shivte. First Chronicles 17:6 reads “judges” (shofte), a very similar word.
That is, a royal dynasty. The Septuagint reads “and the Lord will tell you that you shall build a house to him” (Brenton, modernized).
So the Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint read “before me” (reported).
The Hebrew is obscure, literally “and this is the law of man.” First Chronicles 17:17 reads differently.

The Hebrew is difficult, literally “for you,” “for your land”; compare 1 Chronicles 17:21 and the Septuagint (Brenton, “to do mightily and nobly, so that you should cast out nations and their tabernacles,” modernized).
Literally “found his heart.”

verses.text: After this it came to pass that David struck the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah{a} out of the hand of the Philistines.

He struck Moab and measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to put to death, and one full line to keep alive. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.
David struck also Hadadezer{b} the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power{c} at the river Euphrates.
David took from him a thousand seven hundred horsemen{d} and twenty thousand foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left of them enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Arameans{e} of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand men of the Arameans.
Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became servants to David and brought tribute. And Yahweh gave victory to David wherever he went.
David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.{f}
And from Betah and from Berothai,{g} towns of Hadadezer, King David took a very great quantity of bronze.{h}
When Toi{i} king of Hamath heard that David had struck all the army of Hadadezer,

Toi sent Joram{j} his son to King David to ask after his welfare and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer and struck him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And in his hand were vessels of silver and vessels of gold and vessels of bronze.
These also King David set apart to Yahweh, with the silver and the gold that he had set apart from every nation that he brought under,
from Aram,{k} from Moab, from the Ammonites, from the Philistines, from Amalek, and out of the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down the Arameans{l} in the Valley of Salt, eighteen thousand men.
He put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became servants to David. And Yahweh gave victory to David wherever he went.
So David reigned over all Israel, and David executed justice and righteousness for all his people.
Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat{m} the son of Ahilud was recorder,
and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar{n} were priests, and Seraiah{o} was secretary,
and Benaiah{p} the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites,{q} and David’s sons were priests.{r}

notes.text: Metheg-ammah means “bridle of the mother city” (uncertain); 1 Chronicles 18:1 reads “Gath and its villages.”
Hadadezer means “Hadad is help”; Hadad was the Aramean storm god.
Literally “his hand,” that is, his control or a monument (uncertain).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 18:4 read “a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “Aram” and “Arameans” (Syrians). Likewise throughout.

Or “golden quivers” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “golden bracelets” and adds, “And Susakim king of Egypt took them, when he went up to Jerusalem in the days of Rehoboam son of Solomon” (Brenton, modernized).
Betah is called Tibhath in 1 Chronicles 18:8; the Septuagint reads “Metebac” (Brenton). Berothai means “my wells” (uncertain).
The Septuagint adds “with that Solomon made the bronze sea, and the pillars, and the basins, and all the furnishings” (Brenton, modernized; compare 1 Chronicles 18:8).
Called Tou in 1 Chronicles 18:9. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
Joram means “Yahweh is exalted.” First Chronicles 18:10 reads “Hadoram.”
So the Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint (Brenton, “out of Idumea”), and 1 Chronicles 18:11 read “Edom,” a word very similar in Hebrew.
So the Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts and 1 Chronicles 18:12 read “Edomites”; the Septuagint reads “he smote Idumea” (Brenton). See verse 14.
Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
So the Hebrew. The Syriac reportedly reads “Abiathar son of Ahimelech” (compare 1 Samuel 22:20). Zadok means “righteous.”
Seraiah means “Yahweh has prevailed” (uncertain). He is called Shavsha in 1 Chronicles 18:16.
Benaiah means “Yahweh has built.” Jehoiada means “Yahweh knows.”
The Cherethites and Pelethites were royal guards, perhaps from Crete and Philistia.
Hebrew kohanim, the usual word for priests. First Chronicles 18:17 reads “chief officials at the king’s side”; the Septuagint reads “princes of the court” (Brenton).

verses.text: And David said, “Is there yet any who is left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba,{a} and they called him to David. The king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” And he said, “Your servant is he.”
And the king said, “Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, to whom I may show the kindness of God?” Ziba said to the king, “There is yet a son of Jonathan, lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Look, he is in the house of Machir{b} the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.”{c}
Then King David sent and fetched him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and did obeisance. David said, “Mephibosheth!” And he answered, “Here is your servant!”

David said to him, “Fear not, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat bread at my table continually.”
He bowed himself and said, “What is your servant, that you should look upon such a dead dog as I am?”
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s son.

And you shall till the land for him, you and your sons and your servants, and shall bring in the produce, that your master’s son may have food to eat. But Mephibosheth your master’s son shall eat bread always at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Then Ziba said to the king, “According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do.” “So Mephibosheth ate at my{d} table, as one of the king’s sons.”
Mephibosheth had a young son whose name was Mica.{e} And all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants to Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem, for he ate continually at the king’s table. And he was lame in both his feet.

notes.text: Ziba perhaps means “plant” or “strength” (uncertain).
Machir means “sold.” Ammiel means “my kinsman is God.”
Lo-debar means “no pasture” or “no thing” (uncertain), a town east of the Jordan.
So the Hebrew; the words may be the king’s. The Septuagint reads “at the table of David” (Brenton).
Mica means “who is like?” (short for “who is like Yahweh?”).

verses.text: After this the king of the sons of Ammon died, and Hanun{a} his son reigned in his place.

David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent by the hand of his servants to comfort him concerning his father. And David’s servants came into the land of the sons of Ammon.

But the princes of the sons of Ammon said to Hanun their lord, “Does David honor your father in your eyes, in that he has sent comforters to you? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city, to spy it out, and to overthrow it?”
So Hanun seized David’s servants and shaved away one half of their beards, and he cut away their robes at the middle, up to their hips, and sent them off.
When they told it to David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, “Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”

When the sons of Ammon saw that they had become a stench to David, the sons of Ammon sent and hired twenty thousand footmen from the Arameans of Beth-rehob and from the Arameans of Zobah, and from the king of Maacah a thousand men, and from the men of Tob{b} twelve thousand men.
When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men.
And the sons of Ammon came out and drew up for battle at the entrance of the gate, while the Arameans of Zobah and of Rehob, and the men of Tob and Maacah, were by themselves in the open country.
When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and behind, he chose some of all the choice men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans.
The rest of the people he put into the hand of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the sons of Ammon.
He said, “If the Arameans are too strong for me, then you shall help me; but if the sons of Ammon are too strong for you, then I will come and help you.
Be strong, and let us play the man for our people and for the cities of our God. And may Yahweh do what is good in his eyes.”
So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Arameans, and they fled before him.
When the sons of Ammon saw that the Arameans had fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and went into the city. Then Joab returned from the sons of Ammon and came to Jerusalem.
When the Arameans saw that they had been beaten before Israel, they gathered themselves together.
And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Arameans who were beyond the River,{c} and they came to Helam,{d} with Shobach the captain of the army of Hadadezer at their head.
When it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. And Aram set its ranks in order to meet David, and they fought with him.

And the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed of the Arameans the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen,{e} and he struck Shobach the captain of their army, so that he died there.
When all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been beaten before Israel, they made peace with Israel and served them. So the Arameans feared to help the sons of Ammon any more.

notes.text: Hanun means “favored.”
Or “the men of Ish-tob.” Tob means “good.” The Septuagint reads “Istob” (Brenton) and “the king of Amalek” for “the king of Maacah.” Beth-rehob means “house of the broad place.”
That is, the Euphrates.
Helam was east of the Jordan; its location is uncertain.
First Chronicles 19:18 reads “seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers.” The Septuagint here agrees with the Hebrew (Brenton).

verses.text: Now it came to pass at the return of the year, at the time when kings go out to battle,{a} that David sent Joab and his servants with him and all Israel, and they ravaged the sons of Ammon and besieged Rabbah.{b} But David remained in Jerusalem.

It happened, at the time of evening, that David arose from his couch and walked about on the roof of the king’s house. And from the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very fair to look upon.
David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, “Is not this Bathsheba,{c} the daughter of Eliam,{d} the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”{e}
So David sent messengers and took her, and she came in to him, and he lay with her. (She was cleansing herself from her impurity.) Then she went back to her house.
The woman conceived, and she sent and told David, and said, “I am with child.”
Then David sent to Joab, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” And Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah had come to him, David asked how Joab was faring and how the people fared and how the war went.
David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah went out of the king’s house, and a portion from the king went out after him.
But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.
So they reported to David, “Uriah went not down to his house.” And David asked Uriah, “Is it not from a journey that you come? For what reason did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camped in the open field. Shall I then go into my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? By your life, and by the life of your soul, I will not do this thing.”
Then David said to Uriah, “Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will send you away.” So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.
And David called him, and he ate and drank before him, and he made him drunk. And at evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
He wrote in the letter, saying, “Set Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and withdraw from him, that he may be struck down and die.”
So as Joab was keeping watch on the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew that valiant men were.
And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the people of David’s servants fell. Uriah the Hittite died also.
Then Joab sent and told David all the things concerning the war.
And he charged the messenger, saying, “When you have finished telling all the matters of the war to the king,
then if the king’s anger flares up, and he says to you, ‘For what reason did you approach so close to the city to fight? Did you not know they would shoot from upon the wall?

Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth?{f} Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go near the wall?’ then you shall say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.’”
So the messenger departed, and he came and reported to David everything for which Joab had sent him.{g}
The messenger said to David, “The men prevailed against us and came out against us into the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.
Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king’s servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.”

David said to the messenger, “Thus you shall say to Joab, ‘Let not this matter be evil in your eyes, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your battle against the city and overthrow it.’ And encourage him.”
When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband.
And when the mourning was past, David sent and gathered her into his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.

notes.text: Literally “at the return of the year,” that is, in the spring. So many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint (Brenton, “when the time of the year for kings going out to battle had come round”), and 1 Chronicles 20:1. The traditional Hebrew text reads “messengers” (malʾakhim) for “kings” (melakhim).
Rabbah means “great (city),” the Ammonite capital, modern Amman.
Bathsheba means “daughter of an oath” or “daughter of seven.” She is called Bath-shua in 1 Chronicles 3:5.
Eliam means “God is my kinsman.” He is called Ammiel in 1 Chronicles 3:5.
Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.”
That is, Jerubbaal, Gideon (Judges 6:32; 9:50–54); compare the note on Ish-bosheth at 2:8. The Septuagint reads “Jerobaal son of Ner” (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds a longer form of David’s angry questions, repeating those of verses 20–21 (Brenton).

verses.text: And Yahweh sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, “There were two men in one city, the one rich and the other poor.
The rich man had flocks and herds in great abundance;

but the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and kept alive. And it grew up with him and with his children together. It would eat of his own morsel and drink from his own cup and lie in his bosom, and it was to him as a daughter.

Now a traveler came to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take from his own flock or from his own herd to prepare for the wayfarer who had come to him; but he took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
Then David’s anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As Yahweh lives, the man who did this is a son of death!{a}
And he shall restore the lamb fourfold,{b} because he did this thing and because he had no pity.”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.
I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if that had been too little, I would have added to you as much again.

Why have you despised the word of Yahweh,{c} to do what is evil in his eyes? Uriah the Hittite you have struck with the sword, and his wife you have taken to be your wife, and him you have slain with the sword of the sons of Ammon.
Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.’

Thus says Yahweh: ‘Look, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” And Nathan said to David, “Yahweh also has put away your sin; you shall not die.
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the enemies of Yahweh,{d} the child also who is born to you shall surely die.”
Then Nathan went to his house. And Yahweh struck the child that Uriah’s wife bore to David, and it became very sick.
David therefore sought God for the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.
The elders of his house stood beside him to raise him up from the ground, but he was not willing, and he ate no bread with them.

On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David feared to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “Look, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to our voice. How then shall we tell him that the child is dead? He may do himself some harm.”
But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David perceived that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, “Is the child dead?” They said, “He is dead.”

Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and put on fresh garments. And he entered the house of Yahweh and bowed down. Then he went to his own house, and when he asked, they set bread before him, and he ate.
Then his servants said to him, “What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while it was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate bread.”
He said, “While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows whether Yahweh will be gracious to me, that the child may live?’
But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Then David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon.{e} And Yahweh loved him
and sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah,{f} because of Yahweh.
Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and took the royal city.
And Joab sent messengers to David and said, “I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters.{g}
Now therefore gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and my name be called over it.”
So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it.

He took the crown of their king{h} from his head. Its weight was about seventy-five pounds{i} of gold, with a precious stone, and it was set on David’s head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.

And the people that were in it he brought forth and set them at saws and at sledges of iron and at axes of iron, and made them toil in the brickworks.{j} So he dealt with every city of the sons of Ammon. And David returned with all the people to Jerusalem.

notes.text: That is, deserves to die.
So the Hebrew (compare Exodus 22:1). The Septuagint reads “sevenfold” (reported).
Some Septuagint manuscripts read “despised Yahweh” (reported); compare verse 10.

The Hebrew includes “the enemies of,” probably as a scribal softening to avoid saying David scorned Yahweh himself. The Septuagint reads the same (Brenton, “given great occasion of provocation to the enemies of the Lord”).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “she called.”
Jedidiah means “beloved of Yahweh.” The Septuagint reads “Jeddedi” (Brenton).
That is, the part of the city that controlled the water supply.
Or “of Milcom,” the Ammonite god (1 Kings 11:5); the Hebrew malkam can be read either way. The Septuagint reads “Molchom their king” (Brenton).
Hebrew “a talent,” about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).

So the traditional reading (qere), describing forced labor. The written text (ketiv) reads “made them pass through Malkan,” perhaps a reference to Molech worship (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “put them under the saw … and made them pass through the brick kiln” (Brenton, modernized), which some understand as execution (scholarly review).

verses.text: Now after this it came to pass that Absalom the son of David had a fair sister whose name was Tamar.{a} And Amnon the son of David loved her.
Amnon was so distressed that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed hard in Amnon’s eyes to do anything to her.
But Amnon had a friend whose name was Jonadab,{b} the son of Shimeah, David’s brother. And Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He said to him, “Why are you so lean from morning to morning, son of the king? Will you not tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I love Tamar, the sister of Absalom my brother.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lay yourself upon your bed and make yourself sick. When your father comes in to look on you, tell him, ‘Pray, let Tamar my sister come and feed me with bread, and let her make the dish before my eyes, so that I may watch and eat from her hand.’”

So Amnon lay down and feigned sickness. And the king came in to look on him, and Amnon said to the king, “Pray, let Tamar my sister come and make a couple of cakes before my eyes, that I may eat from her hand.”
Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, “Go now to your brother Amnon’s house and prepare food for him.”
So Tamar went to the house of Amnon her brother, and he was lying in bed. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.
And she took the pan and poured them out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, “Send everyone out from me.” So everyone went out from him.
Then Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand.” And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.
But when she brought them near to him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, “Come, lie with me, my sister.”
She answered him, “No, my brother, do not humble me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this outrage.{c}
And I, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, I pray you, speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.”
But he would not listen to her voice. Being stronger than she, he forced her and lay with her.
Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, “Get up, go!”
But she said to him, “No, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me.”{d} But he would not listen to her.
Then he summoned the lad who attended him and said, “Send this one away from me, out of doors, and fasten the door behind her.”
She had on her a long-sleeved tunic,{e} for in such robes the king’s daughters who were virgins were dressed. So his attendant put her outside and fastened the door behind her.
And Tamar put ashes on her head and rent the long-sleeved tunic that was on her. And she put her hand upon her head and went off, crying out as she walked.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has Amnon your brother{f} been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this thing to heart.” So Tamar dwelt, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom’s house.
When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.{g}
But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had humbled his sister Tamar.
Two whole years later, Absalom held a sheep-shearing in Baal-hazor near Ephraim, and he called all the sons of the king.
Absalom came to the king and said, “See now, your servant has sheepshearers. Let the king, I pray, and his servants go with your servant.”
The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, let us not all go now, lest we be burdensome to you.” He pressed him, but he would not go, though he blessed him.
Then Absalom said, “If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us.” And the king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king’s sons go with him.{h}

Then Absalom commanded his young men, saying, “Mark now, when Amnon’s heart is merry with wine, and I say to you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ then kill him. Do not fear. Have not I commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant.”
So the young men of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king’s sons arose, and each man mounted his mule and fled.
While they were on the road, the tidings reached David: “Absalom has slain every one of the king’s sons, and there is not one of them left.”
Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants stood by with their clothes torn.

But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David’s brother, answered and said, “Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king’s sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command{i} of Absalom this has been determined from the day he humbled his sister Tamar.
Now therefore let not my lord the king take the thing to his heart, to think that all the king’s sons are dead; for Amnon alone is dead.”
But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and look, a great company was approaching on the road behind him{j} along the hillside.
Jonadab said to the king, “See, the king’s sons are coming. According to your servant’s word, so it has come to be.”
As soon as he had finished speaking, look, the king’s sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.
But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud,{k} king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.
So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.
And the spirit of King David longed to go out{l} to Absalom, for he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.

notes.text: Tamar means “palm tree.”
Jonadab means “Yahweh is generous.” Shimeah is called Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9 and Shimea in 1 Chronicles 2:13.
Hebrew nevalah, a word for gross folly or sacrilege; compare verse 13, “fools” (nevalim).
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Or “a robe reaching to the palms and soles” (uncertain); the same phrase describes Joseph’s robe (Genesis 37:3).
Hebrew “Aminon,” perhaps a diminutive or a scornful form.
The Septuagint adds “but he did not grieve the spirit of his son Amnon, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn” (Brenton, modernized). 4QSam-a reportedly contains the same addition.
The Septuagint adds “and Absalom made a banquet like the banquet of the king” (Brenton, modernized).
Literally “mouth.”
So the Hebrew; the meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint adds “by the way of Horonaim” (Brenton, “by the way of Oronen,” modernized) and a report to the king.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “Ammihur.” The Septuagint adds “to the land of Chamaachad” (Brenton).

The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “and David the king was spent to go out to Absalom.” 4QSam-a reportedly reads “the spirit of the king.” The Septuagint reads “King David ceased to go out after Absalom” (Brenton).

verses.text: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart went out to Absalom.{a}

And Joab sent to Tekoa{b} and fetched from there a wise woman and said to her, “Act the part of a mourner, I pray, and clothe yourself in garments of mourning, and do not rub yourself with oil, but be as a woman who has grieved for the dead a long time.
Go to the king and speak thus to him.” So Joab put the words in her mouth.
When the woman of Tekoa spoke{c} to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and did obeisance and said, “Save, O king!”
And the king said to her, “What troubles you?” She answered, “Truly I am a widow; my husband is dead.
And your handmaid had two sons, and they quarreled together in the field. There was no one to part them, and the one struck the other and killed him.

And now the whole clan has risen against your handmaid, and they say, ‘Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.’ So they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal which is left, and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant upon the face of the earth.”
Then the king said to the woman, “Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you.”
And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, “On me be the iniquity, my lord the king, and on my father’s house; and let the king and his throne be guiltless.”
The king said, “Whoever speaks to you, bring him to me, and he shall not touch you any more.”

Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood may destroy no more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”
Then the woman said, “Let your handmaid, I pray, speak a word to my lord the king.” He said, “Speak.”

And the woman said, “Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in speaking this word the king is as one who is guilty, in that the king does not bring home again his banished one.

For we must surely die, and are as water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away a life; he devises means so that the banished one is not cast out from him.

Now the reason I have come to speak this word to my lord the king is that the people have made me afraid. And your handmaid said, ‘I will speak now to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.
For the king will listen, to rescue his handmaid out of the grasp of the man who seeks to cut off both me and my son together from God’s inheritance.’
Then your handmaid said, ‘Let the word of my lord the king be for rest,’ for as a messenger{d} of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and evil. And may Yahweh your God be with you!”
Then the king answered and said to the woman, “Do not hide from me, I pray, anything that I ask you.” And the woman said, “Let my lord the king speak.”

The king said, “Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?” The woman answered and said, “As your soul lives, my lord the king, none can turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has spoken. For it was your servant Joab who charged me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your handmaid.
To change the face of the matter your servant Joab has done this thing. But my lord is wise, according to the wisdom of a messenger of God, to know all things that are in the earth.”
Then the king said to Joab, “Look now, I have done this thing. Go therefore, bring back the young man Absalom.”

And Joab fell on his face to the ground and did obeisance and blessed the king. And Joab said, “Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, in that the king has performed the request of his servant.”
So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “Let him turn to his own house; but my face he shall not see.” So Absalom turned to his own house and did not see the king’s face.
Now in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

And when he polled his head (it was at every year’s end that he polled it, because it weighed heavily on him; therefore he polled it), he weighed the hair of his head, about five pounds{e} by the king’s weight.
There were born to Absalom three sons and one daughter, whose name was Tamar. She was a woman fair to look upon.{f}
So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem without seeing the king’s face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but he would not come to him. And he sent again a second time, but he would not come.
Therefore he said to his servants, “See, Joab’s field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.{g}
Then Joab arose and came to Absalom at his house and said to him, “Why have your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom answered Joab, “Look, I sent to you, saying, ‘Come here, that I may send you to the king to say, “Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still.”’ Now therefore let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him put me to death.”
So Joab went to the king and told him. And he called for Absalom. He came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.

notes.text: Or “was against Absalom.” The Hebrew can be read either way.
Tekoa was a town about 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of Bethlehem, later the home of the prophet Amos.
So many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and other versions (reported). The traditional Hebrew text reads “said.”
Or “angel.” Likewise in verse 20.
Hebrew “200 shekels,” about 5 pounds (2.3 kilograms). The Septuagint likewise reads “two hundred shekels according to the royal shekel” (Brenton).

The Septuagint adds, “and she becomes the wife of Rehoboam son of Solomon, and she bears to him Abijah” (Brenton, modernized). Compare 1 Kings 15:2, where Abijah’s mother is called Maacah daughter of Abishalom.

The Septuagint, and 4QSam-a reportedly, add “And the servants of Joab came to him with their clothes torn, and they said to him, ‘The servants of Absalom have set the field on fire’” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: After this it came about that Absalom prepared for himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.

Absalom used to rise early and stand by the side of the road to the gate. And whenever anyone had a case that was to go up to the king for a ruling, Absalom would summon him and ask, “From which town do you come?” And when he said, “Your servant is of such and such a tribe of Israel,”
then Absalom would tell him, “Look, your matters are sound and just, but there is none from the king to give you a hearing.”
Absalom would say moreover, “O that I were made judge in the land! Then every man who had a dispute or a cause might come to me, and I would do him justice.”
And whenever a man came near to do him obeisance, he would stretch out his hand and seize him and kiss him.
In this manner Absalom did to all Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
At the end of forty years{a} Absalom said to the king, “Let me go, I pray, and pay my vow, which I have vowed to Yahweh, in Hebron.
For your servant vowed a vow while I dwelt at Geshur in Aram, saying, ‘If Yahweh will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will serve Yahweh.’”{b}
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he arose and went to Hebron.
But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “As soon as you hear the sound of the horn, then you shall say, ‘Absalom is king in Hebron!’”
Now with Absalom went two hundred men out of Jerusalem, men who had been called, and they went in their simplicity and knew nothing at all.

And while he was offering the sacrifices, Absalom sent for Ahithophel{c} the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city, from Giloh. So the plot became mighty, for the people with Absalom grew ever more in number.
A messenger came to David, saying, “The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom.”

Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, “Arise, and let us flee, for otherwise there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Make haste to depart, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down evil on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”
The king’s servants said to the king, “Look, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king shall choose.”
So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house.
And the king went out, and all the people after him, and they halted at the Far House.{d}
All his servants passed on beside him, and all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men who had followed him from Gath, passed on before the king.{e}
Then the king said to Ittai{f} the Gittite, “Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your own place.

Yesterday was your coming, and today shall I make you go up and down with us, when I myself go wherever I can go? Return, and take back your brothers with you. Steadfast love and faithfulness be with you.”{g}
But Ittai answered the king, “As Yahweh lives, and as my lord the king lives, surely in whatever place my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be.”
David said to Ittai, “Go on and cross over.” So Ittai of Gath went across, with all his men and all the children who were with him.
And the whole country was weeping with a great voice while all the people crossed over. And the king went over the brook Kidron,{h} and all the people passed on toward the way of the wilderness.

And look, Zadok also came, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar went up,{i} until all the people had finished passing out of the city.
Then the king said to Zadok, “Carry back the ark of God into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of Yahweh, he will cause me to return and will show me it and the place where it dwells.
But if he says thus, ‘I have no delight in you,’ here I am; let him do to me as seems good to him.”
The king said also to Zadok the priest, “Are you a seer?{j} Return in peace to the city, you and your two sons with you, Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan son of Abiathar.
See, I will wait at the fords{k} of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.”
Zadok therefore and Abiathar returned the ark of God to Jerusalem, and there they stayed.

But David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up, with his head covered, and he went barefoot. And all the people who were with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went.
And one told David, saying, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” And David said, “O Yahweh, I pray you, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”
When David came to the summit, where God was worshiped, look, Hushai{l} the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and earth upon his head.
David said to him, “If you pass on with me, you will be a burden to me.

But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘Your servant I will be, O king; I was your father’s servant formerly, and now I am yours,’ then you shall bring to nothing for me the advice of Ahithophel.
And are there not with you Zadok and Abiathar the priests? So it shall be that every word you hear out of the king’s house, you shall report it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
Look, they have there with them their two sons, Ahimaaz of Zadok and Jonathan of Abiathar; and by their hand you shall send me every word you hear.”
So Hushai, David’s friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was coming into Jerusalem.

notes.text: So the Hebrew and the Septuagint (Brenton, “after forty years”). Some Septuagint manuscripts, the Syriac, and Josephus reportedly read “four years,” which fits the context better (scholarly review).
Some Septuagint manuscripts reportedly add “in Hebron.”
Ahithophel means “brother of folly” (uncertain), perhaps a scribal alteration. Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah. The Septuagint reads “the Theconite … from Gola” (Brenton).
Hebrew Beth-merhak, perhaps the last house of the city.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. The Septuagint has a longer text (Brenton).
Ittai means “with me” (uncertain).
So the Septuagint (reported). The Hebrew reads “take back your brothers with you, steadfast love and faithfulness.”
Kidron means “dark” or “turbid,” the valley east of Jerusalem.
Or “offered sacrifices.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew is uncertain; perhaps “Do you see?” The Septuagint reads “Behold, you shall return” (Brenton, modernized).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “the plains.”
Hushai means “quick” (uncertain).

verses.text: When David had passed a little beyond the summit, look, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with a couple of donkeys saddled, and on them two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits,{a} and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “What do you mean by these?” Ziba said, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for any who grow faint in the wilderness.”
And the king said, “And where is your master’s son?” Ziba said to the king, “Look, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.’”
Then the king said to Ziba, “Look, everything of Mephibosheth’s is yours.” And Ziba said, “I bow myself; may I find grace in your sight, my lord the king.”
When King David came to Bahurim,{b} look, there came out from there a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei{c} the son of Gera. Coming out, he kept cursing as he came.
And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, while all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.
And thus said Shimei as he cursed: “Go out, go out, man of bloodshed, base fellow!{d}

Yahweh has returned upon you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and Yahweh has given the kingdom into the hand of Absalom your son. See, you are taken in your own evil, for you are a man of blood.”
Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over, I pray, and take off his head.”
But the king said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because{e} Yahweh has said to him, ‘Curse David,’ who then shall say, ‘Why have you done so?’”

And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, “Look, my son who came forth from my body seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjamite! Let him alone, and let him curse, for Yahweh has bidden him.
It may be that Yahweh will look on my affliction,{f} and that Yahweh will repay me with good for his cursing this day.”
So David and his men went along the road, and Shimei walked along the side of the hill alongside him, cursing as he walked, and he hurled stones over against him and threw dust.
And the king and all the people who were with him arrived weary,{g} and he refreshed himself there.
Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this the kindness you show your companion? Why did you not go with your companion?”
Hushai said to Absalom, “No, but whom Yahweh and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his will I be, and with him I will remain.
And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served in your father’s presence, so will I be in your presence.”
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give your counsel. What shall we do?”
