Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines, whom he has left to keep the house. All Israel will then hear that you have become a stench to your father, and the hands of all your supporters will grow strong.”
They spread for Absalom the tent upon the housetop, and Absalom went in unto his father’s concubines before the eyes of all Israel.
Now the counsel of Ahithophel, which he gave in those days, was as if one inquired at the word of God. So was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.

notes.text: Probably cakes of summer fruit such as figs. The Septuagint reads “a hundred cakes of dates” (Brenton).
Bahurim means “young men,” a village east of Jerusalem near the Mount of Olives.
Shimei means “heard” (short for “Yahweh has heard”). Gera means “grain” (uncertain).
Hebrew “man of Belial.”
So the traditional reading (qere). The written text reads “If he curses, and if.”
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “look on my affliction”) and other ancient versions. The written Hebrew text reads “on my iniquity”; the traditional reading (qere) reads “on my eye,” perhaps “my tears.”
The Hebrew reads “arrived weary” without naming a place; perhaps a place name, ʿAyephim, has dropped out (compare 17:22, “the Jordan”).

verses.text: Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me now choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David this night.
I will come upon him while he is weary and his hands are slack, and I will make him tremble, and all the people who are with him will flee. And I will strike the king alone.
And I will bring back all the people to you. The man whom you seek is as the return of all;{a} so all the people shall be at peace.”
And the saying pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Then Absalom said, “Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what is in his mouth.”
When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom spoke to him, saying, “Thus has Ahithophel spoken. Shall we do according to his word? If not, you speak.”
Then Hushai said to Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai said moreover, “You know your father and his men, that they are mighty men, and they are bitter of soul, like a bear robbed of her whelps in the field. And your father is a man of war; he will not lodge with the people.

Look, he is hidden now in one of the pits or in some other place. And it will come to pass, when some of them fall at the first, that whoever hears it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.’
Then even the valiant man, whose heart is as the heart of a lion, will utterly melt. For all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and those who are with him are valiant men.
Therefore I counsel that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan even to Beersheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in your own person.{b}

So shall we come upon him in some place where he shall be found, and we will light upon him as the dew falls on the ground. And of him and of all the men who are with him there shall not be left even one.
And if he gathers himself into a town, then all Israel will carry cords to that town, and we will haul it down into the ravine, until not even a pebble is found there.”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For Yahweh had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that Yahweh might bring evil upon Absalom.
Then Hushai said to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, “Thus and thus did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and thus have I counseled.

Now therefore send quickly and tell David, saying, ‘Do not lodge this night at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king be swallowed up, and all the people who are with him.’”

Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying at En-rogel.{c} And a maidservant would go and bring them word, and they in turn would go and bring word to King David; for they dared not be seen entering the city.
But a lad saw them and told Absalom. So the two of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man in Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
And the woman took a covering and spread it over the well’s mouth and scattered grain on it, and the thing was not known.

When Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house, they said, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” And the woman said to them, “They have gone over the brook of water.”{d} And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.
After they had departed, the men came up out of the well and went and told King David. They said to David, “Arise and cross quickly over the water, for thus has Ahithophel counseled against you.”
Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By the morning light not one of them was lacking who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and arose and went home to his city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father.
Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him.
Absalom set Amasa{e} over the army in place of Joab. Now Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite,{f} who had gone in to Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, and Barzillai{g} the Gileadite of Rogelim,
brought couches, bowls, and pottery vessels, also wheat and barley, meal and roasted grain, beans and lentils and roasted seeds,{h}
honey and curds and sheep, and cheese of the herd, for David and the people who were with him to eat. For they said, “The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.”

notes.text: The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “as a bride returns to her husband: only you seek the life of one man” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “your face going into battle.” Some ancient versions reportedly read “in their midst.”
En-rogel means “spring of the fuller” (uncertain), just south of Jerusalem.
The meaning of the Hebrew word mikhal is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “gone a little way beyond the water” (Brenton).
Amasa means “burden” (uncertain).
So the Hebrew. First Chronicles 2:17 reads “Jether the Ishmaelite”; the Septuagint reads “Jether of Jezreel” (Brenton). Abigal is a form of Abigail.
Shobi perhaps means “captor” (uncertain). Barzillai means “man of iron.” Rogelim means “fullers.”
The Hebrew repeats “parched grain”; the Septuagint lacks the repetition (reported).

verses.text: Then David mustered the people who were with him and set over them captains of thousands and captains of hundreds.

And David sent out the people, a third under the hand of Joab, a third under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the people, “I will surely go out with you myself also.”

But the people said, “You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not set their heart on us; if half of us die, they will not set their heart on us. But you are worth ten thousand of us.{a} Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city.”
The king said to them, “What seems best to you I will do.” So the king stood by the side of the gate, while all the people went out by hundreds and by thousands.

And the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, “Deal gently for my sake with the young man, with Absalom.” And all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge concerning Absalom.
So the people went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was in the forest of Ephraim.{b}
The people of Israel were beaten there before the servants of David, and there was a great slaughter there that day, twenty thousand men.
For the battle there was spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword devoured.

Absalom chanced upon the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule passed beneath the tangled boughs of a great oak, and his head was caught fast in the oak, and he was hung up{c} between the heavens and the earth, and the mule beneath him passed on.
And a certain man saw it and told Joab, “Look, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
Joab said to the man who told him, “And look, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him down there to the ground? It would have been on me to give you ten pieces of silver{d} and a belt.”

But the man said to Joab, “Though I should feel in my hand a thousand pieces of silver,{e} yet I would not put forth my hand against the king’s son. For in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, saying, ‘Protect,{f} for me, the young man Absalom.’
Else, had I wrought treachery against his life{g}—and no matter is hid from the king—you yourself would have stood off from me.”
Then Joab said, “I may not linger thus with you.” And he took three darts{h} in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.
And ten young men who carried Joab’s armor surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.
Then Joab blew the horn, and the people returned from pursuing after Israel, for Joab held back the people.
They took Absalom and cast him into the great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each man to his tent.

Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar which is in the King’s Valley, for he said, “I have no son to keep my name in remembrance.”{i} And he called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Monument to this day.
Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, “Let me now run and carry the king tidings, how Yahweh has delivered him from the hand of his enemies.”
Joab said to him, “You shall not be the bearer of tidings this day; you shall bear tidings another day. But this day you shall bear no tidings, because the king’s son is dead.”
Then Joab said to the Cushite,{j} “Go, tell the king what you have seen.” The Cushite bowed himself to Joab and ran.

Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, “Come what may, let me also, I pray, run after the Cushite.” Joab said, “Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the tidings?”
“Come what may,” he said, “I will run.” So he said to him, “Run.” Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain{k} and outran the Cushite.
Now David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof over the gate by the wall, and he lifted up his eyes and looked, and there was a man running alone.
The watchman cried out and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, there are tidings in his mouth.” And he kept coming and drawing near.
Then the watchman saw another man running, and the watchman called to the gatekeeper and said, “Look, another man running alone!” The king said, “He also brings tidings.”
The watchman said, “I think the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok.” And the king said, “He is a good man and comes with good tidings.”

Then Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, “All is well!”{l} And he bowed himself before the king with his face to the earth and said, “Blessed be Yahweh your God, who has delivered up the men who lifted up their hand against my lord the king!”
The king said, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?” Ahimaaz answered, “When Joab sent the king’s servant and me your servant, I saw a great tumult, but I did not know what it was.”
The king said, “Turn aside and stand here.” So he turned aside and stood still.
And look, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, “Let my lord the king receive tidings! For Yahweh has judged for you today against the hand of all those rising against you.”

The king said to the Cushite, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?” The Cushite answered, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you to do you harm, be as that young man is.”

And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, thus he said: “O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would that I had died in your place, O Absalom, my son, my son!”{m}

notes.text: So two Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint (Brenton, “you are as ten thousand of us”), and the Vulgate (reported). The traditional Hebrew text reads “for now there are ten thousand like us.”
The forest of Ephraim was east of the Jordan, in Gilead, despite its name.
So the Septuagint and other ancient versions (reported). The Hebrew reads “he was set.”
Hebrew “ten of silver,” that is, ten shekels, about 4 ounces (115 grams).
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms). The Septuagint reads “a thousand shekels of silver” (Brenton).
So some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions (reported), reading “for me.” The traditional text reads “whoever you are.”
So the written Hebrew text (ketiv); the traditional reading (qere) is “my life.” Marked for scholarly review.
Hebrew “three sticks” or “three rods”; perhaps spears or javelins.
Compare 14:27, which says Absalom had three sons; perhaps they died young.
That is, a man from Cush, the region south of Egypt (Nubia).
That is, the plain of the Jordan Valley.
Hebrew “Peace!”
In Hebrew this verse is 19:1, and 19:1–43 in English is 19:2–44 in Hebrew. The Septuagint follows the Hebrew numbering (Brenton).

verses.text: It was told Joab, “Look, the king weeps and mourns for Absalom.”{a}
So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard it said that day, “The king grieves for his son.”
And the people crept into the city on that day, the way a people creeps in that is put to shame by fleeing in the fight.
But the king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, “O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!”

Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, “Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants, who this day have saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and the lives of your concubines,

in that you love your haters and hate your lovers. For you have made known today that princes and servants count for nothing with you. For this day I know that had Absalom lived and we all died this day, that would have been pleasing in your sight.

Now then, rise, go forth and speak kindly to your servants. For by Yahweh I swear, unless you go forth, not one man will stay the night with you; and that will be a greater evil to you than every evil that has come upon you from your youth until now.”

Then the king arose and sat in the gate. And they told all the people, saying, “Look, the king is sitting in the gate.” And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled, every man to his tent.

And all the people were in strife throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom.
But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in the battle. So now, why are you silent about returning the king?”

And King David sent to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah, saying, ‘Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king, even to his house?{b}
You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?’
And say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you shall not be commander of the army before me continually in the place of Joab.’”
So he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, and they sent word to the king, “Return, you and all your servants.”
So the king returned and came to the Jordan. And Judah came to Gilgal to go to meet the king, to bring the king over the Jordan.
And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, who was from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
And a thousand men of Benjamin were with him, and Ziba the servant of Saul’s house, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they rushed down to the Jordan before the king.
And they crossed the ford{c} to bring over the king’s household and to do what was good in his eyes. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king as he was about to cross the Jordan,

and he said to the king, “Let not my lord reckon iniquity to me, nor remember how your servant did perversely on the day my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, look, I have come today, the first of all the house of Joseph, to go down to meet my lord the king.”
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, “Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the anointed of Yahweh?”

But David said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day become an adversary{d} to me? Shall any man be put to death in Israel today? Am I not sure that today I am king over Israel?”
Then the king told Shimei, “You will not die,” and the king gave him his oath.

Then Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had not dressed his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace.
And when he came from Jerusalem{e} to meet the king, the king asked him, “For what reason did you not go along with me, Mephibosheth?”
He answered, “My lord, O king, my servant deceived me. For your servant said, ‘I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king,’ because your servant is lame.
And he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is as an angel of God. Do therefore what is good in your eyes.

For all my father’s house were nothing but men of death before my lord the king, yet you placed your servant with those eating at your table. What right more have I, that I should still cry to the king?”
The king said to him, “Why speak any more of your affairs? I have said, ‘You and Ziba shall divide the land.’”
And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Indeed, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely to his own house.”
Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he crossed to the Jordan with the king, to send him on his way across the Jordan.
Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man.
And the king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem.”
But Barzillai said to the king, “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or what I drink? Can I hear any longer the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be yet a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant would go just a little way over the Jordan with the king. And why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Let your servant, I pray, turn back again, that I may die in my own city, by the grave of my father and my mother. But look, here is your servant Chimham.{f} Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you.”
And the king answered, “Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him whatever is good in your eyes; and all that you choose to ask of me, that will I do for you.”
Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah brought the king over, and also half the people of Israel.

And look, all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, “Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David’s men with him?”

All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, “Because the king is near of kin to us. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king’s cost? Or has any gift been given to us?”

And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, “Ten parts in the king are ours, and in David too we have a greater claim than you.{g} Why then have you made light of us? Was not our word the first to bring back our king?” But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.

notes.text: English 19:1–43 is Hebrew 19:2–44; English 18:33 is Hebrew 19:1. The Septuagint follows the Hebrew numbering.
The Hebrew places the clause “when the word of all Israel has come to the king” at the end of the verse; the Septuagint has it in the same place (Brenton).
Hebrew uncertain; perhaps “And the ferry crossed over.”
Or “a satan,” that is, an accuser or opponent.
Or “came to Jerusalem.”
Chimham perhaps means “longing” (uncertain). He is apparently Barzillai’s son (compare 1 Kings 2:7).
The Septuagint reads “we are older than you” (Brenton); some scholars reportedly prefer “we are the firstborn rather than you.”

verses.text: Now there happened to be there a worthless man{a} whose name was Sheba{b} the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the horn and said, “We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!”
So all the men of Israel withdrew from following David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah clung to their king, from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten women, his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and placed them in a house of ward and fed them, yet he went not in unto them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as in widowhood.
Then the king said to Amasa, “Summon me the men of Judah within three days, and you yourself be present here.”
So Amasa went to call Judah together, but he delayed beyond the set time which had been appointed him.

And David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord’s servants and pursue after him, lest he find for himself fortified cities and escape out of our sight.”{c}
And there went out after him Joab’s men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue after Sheba the son of Bichri.

When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was girded in his soldier’s garment, and over it was a belt with a sword fastened upon his loins in its sheath; and as he went forward, it fell out.
And Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

But Amasa paid no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand. So he struck him with it in the belly and poured out his entrails to the ground, and did not strike him a second time, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.
And one of Joab’s young men stood over him and said, “He who delights in Joab, and he who is David’s, let him go after Joab.”

And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the highway. And when the man saw that all the people stood still, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him, since he saw that everyone who came by him stood still.
When he was removed from the highway, every man went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah,{d} and all the Bichrites{e} gathered together and followed him in also.

And they came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart. And all the people who were with Joab were battering the wall to throw it down.
Then a wise woman cried from the city, “Hear, hear! Say, I pray you, to Joab, ‘Come near here, that I may speak with you.’”
He came near to her, and the woman said, “Are you Joab?” He answered, “I am.” Then she said to him, “Hear the words of your maidservant.” And he said, “I am listening.”
Then she spoke, saying, “They used to speak in former times, saying, ‘Let them but ask counsel at Abel,’ and so they ended the matter.{f}
I am of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the inheritance of Yahweh?”
Joab answered and said, “Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy!

The matter is not so. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, has lifted up his hand against the king, against David. Only hand him over, and I will depart from the city.” And the woman said to Joab, “Look, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall.”

Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the horn, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his tents. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
Now Joab was over all the army of Israel, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites,
and Adoram{g} was in charge of the labor gangs, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder,
and Sheva was secretary, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests,
and also Ira the Jairite{h} was a priest to David.

notes.text: Hebrew “a man of belial.”
Sheba perhaps means “seven” or “oath” (uncertain). Bichri perhaps means “youthful” or “firstborn” (uncertain).
Hebrew uncertain; literally “and snatch away our eye.” The Septuagint reads “so he will blind our eyes” (Brenton, modernized).
Abel of Beth-maacah means “meadow of the house of Maacah,” in the far north.
So the Hebrew; some ancient versions reportedly read “Berites” or “all the choice men.”
The Septuagint reads a longer saying about asking in Abel and in Dan whether the faithful in Israel had failed (Brenton); some scholars reportedly think “and in Dan” is original.
Adoram is a shortened form of Adoniram (1 Kings 4:6), the reading of the Septuagint (Brenton).
The Septuagint reads “Iras the son of Iarin” (Brenton). Jairite refers to the clan of Jair, a Manassite (Numbers 32:41).

verses.text: Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year following year. And David sought the face of Yahweh. And Yahweh said, “It is on account of Saul and his house of blood, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”

So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not of the sons of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites, and the sons of Israel had sworn to them;{a} yet Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the sons of Israel and Judah.
And David said to the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? And with what shall I make atonement, that you may bless the inheritance of Yahweh?”

The Gibeonites said to him, “It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel.” And he said, “Whatever you say, I will do for you.”
They said to the king, “The man who consumed us and who planned against us, that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the borders of Israel,
let seven men of his sons be given to us, and we will hang them up{b} to Yahweh at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of Yahweh.”{c} And the king said, “I will give them.”
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the oath of Yahweh that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Merab{d} the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

And he gave them into the hand of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before Yahweh, and the seven of them fell together. They were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, at the start of barley harvest.{e}

Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water poured upon them from the heavens. And she let neither the birds of the air settle on them by day nor the beasts of the field by night.
When it was told David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done,

David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the lords of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the open square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them on the day the Philistines struck down Saul at Gilboa.
And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son, and they gathered the bones of those who were hanged.

And they buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin in Zela,{f} in the tomb of Kish his father. And they did all that the king commanded. And after that God was moved by entreaty for the land.
The Philistines had war again with Israel, and David went down, and his servants with him, and they fought against the Philistines. And David grew weary.
And Ishbi-benob,{g} who was one of the descendants of the giants,{h} whose spearhead weighed about 7½ pounds{i} of bronze, and who was girded with something new,{j} thought to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah helped him, and he struck down the Philistine and slew him. Then the men of David took an oath to him, saying, “Never again shall you go forth with us into battle, lest you put out the lamp of Israel.”
And it came to pass after this that there was once more war with the Philistines at Gob. At that time Sibbecai the Hushathite slew Saph, who was among the offspring of the giants.
And there was again a battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, slew Goliath of Gath,{k} and the wood of his spear was like a weaver’s beam.
And there was again a battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number; and he also was born to the giant.
And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei,{l} David’s brother, struck him down.
These four were born to the giant in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.

notes.text: See Joshua 9:3–27.
The exact form of execution is uncertain; perhaps “impale” or “expose.” So also verses 9 and 13.

So the Hebrew. Some scholars, following a reported reading, emend to “on the mountain of Yahweh” (compare verse 9). The Septuagint reads “in Gibeon of Saul, as chosen out for the Lord” (Brenton, modernized).

So two Hebrew manuscripts and some Septuagint manuscripts (reported); compare 1 Samuel 18:19. Most Hebrew manuscripts and Brenton’s Septuagint read “Michal.” Armoni perhaps means “of the palace” (uncertain).
Barley harvest fell in April–May.
Zela perhaps means “rib” or “side” (uncertain).
So the traditional reading (qere). Ishbi-benob perhaps means “his dwelling is in Nob” (uncertain).
Hebrew “the Rapha” or “the Raphah,” the ancestor of a race of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11); so also verses 18, 20, and 22.
Hebrew “three hundred shekels,” about 7½ pounds (3.4 kilograms). The Septuagint also reads “three hundred shekels of brass” (Brenton).
Hebrew “girded with a new [thing]”; the noun is missing. The Septuagint reads “girded with a club” (Brenton).

First Chronicles 20:5 reads “Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite.” Compare 1 Samuel 17, where David kills Goliath. “Oregim” means “weavers” and may have been copied from the end of the verse. Marked for scholarly review.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “Shimei”; elsewhere he is called Shimeah (13:3) or Shammah (1 Samuel 16:9).

verses.text: And David spoke to Yahweh the words of this song on the day when Yahweh delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.{a}
He said: “Yahweh is my crag and my stronghold and my deliverer,
my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield and the horn{b} of my salvation, my high retreat and my place of flight, my savior; from violence you save me.
I call upon Yahweh, who is to be praised, and from my enemies I am saved.
“For the breakers of death encircled me; the torrents of worthlessness{c} terrified me;
the cords of Sheol{d} surrounded me; the snares of death came to meet me.
When I was hemmed in, I cried out to Yahweh; unto my God I cried. Out of his temple my voice was heard by him; my cry for help reached his ears.
“Then the earth heaved and rocked; the bases of the heavens quivered and tottered, for his anger burned.
Smoke went up from his nostrils, and fire from his mouth devoured; coals were kindled by it.
He bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet.
He rode upon a cherub and flew; he was seen{e} upon the wings of the wind.
He made darkness around him his shelters, a gathering of waters, thick clouds of the skies.
From the brightness before him coals of fire were kindled.
Yahweh thundered from the heavens, and the Most High gave forth his voice.
He sent out arrows and scattered them, lightning, and routed them.
Then the channels of the sea appeared; the foundations of the world were laid bare at the rebuke of Yahweh, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
“He sent from on high; he took me; he drew me out of many waters.
He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me.
They came upon me in the day of my calamity, but Yahweh was my support.
He led me forth into a wide space; he set me free, for he took pleasure in me.
“Yahweh dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he repaid me.
For I have kept the ways of Yahweh, and have not done wickedly against my God.
For all his rulings were in front of me, and his decrees I did not put away from me.
I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my iniquity.
And Yahweh has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness before his eyes.
“To the faithful one you are faithful; to the mighty man of integrity you deal with integrity;
to the cleansed one you deal cleanly, but to the twisted one you deal shrewdly.
And the afflicted people you save, but your eyes are upon the haughty, to bring them low.
For you are my lamp, O Yahweh, and Yahweh lights up my darkness.
For with you I rush upon a raiding band; with my God I spring over a rampart.
This God—his way is blameless; the word of Yahweh is refined; he is a shield to all who take refuge in him.
“For who is God, besides Yahweh? And who is a rock, besides our God?
This God is my strong fortress,{f} and he sets the blameless free in his way.{g}
He makes my feet like the feet of does, and sets me upon my high places.
He teaches my hands to make war, and my arms bend a bronze bow.
You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your answering{h} has made me great.
You widened my stride beneath me, and my ankles did not slip.
I chased my foes and wiped them out; I turned not back till I had made an end of them.
I consumed them; I shattered them, so that they did not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
For you girded me with strength for battle; you made those who rose against me bow down beneath me.
You gave me the necks of my foes; my haters—I put an end to them.
They looked, but there was none to save; they cried to Yahweh, but he did not answer them.
I beat them fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and stamped them like the mire of the streets.
“You delivered me from the strivings of my people;{i} you kept me as the head of the nations; a people whom I had not known served me.
Sons of a foreign land came cringing to me; at the hearing of the ear they hearkened to me.
Sons of a foreign land faded away and came quaking{j} from their strongholds.
“Yahweh lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be my God, the rock of my salvation,
the God who gives me vengeance and brings down peoples under me,
who brings me out from my enemies. You lift me up above those who rise against me; you deliver me from the man of violence.
For this I will praise you, O Yahweh, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.
He is a tower of salvation{k} for his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and to his offspring forever.”

notes.text: This song closely parallels Psalm 18, with many small differences in wording.
“Horn” is a figure for strength.
Hebrew “belial.”
Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead.
So the Hebrew; Psalm 18:10 and some Hebrew manuscripts read “he soared” (reported). The Septuagint reads “was seen” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; Psalm 18:32 reads “who girds me with strength,” and the Septuagint here reads “who strengthens me with might” (Brenton).
Hebrew uncertain; perhaps “and has made my way blameless” (compare Psalm 18:32), so the Septuagint (Brenton).
Or “your humility,” “your condescension”; Psalm 18:35 reads “your gentleness.” The Septuagint reads “your propitious dealing” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Psalm 18:43 read “the people” (reported).
So Psalm 18:45; the Hebrew here reads “girded themselves” (uncertain).
So the traditional reading (qere), as in Psalm 18:50 “great salvation”; the written text reads “He is a tower.” Marked for scholarly review.

verses.text: Now these are the last words of David: “The utterance of David the son of Jesse, the utterance of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet singer of Israel:{a}
“The Spirit of Yahweh speaks by me; his word is upon my tongue.
The God of Israel has said; the Rock of Israel has spoken to me: ‘One who rules over men justly, ruling in the fear of God,
is like the light of morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, when from brightness after rain the tender grass springs out of the earth.’
“For is not my house so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secured. For will he not cause to sprout all my salvation and all my desire?{b}
But worthless men{c} are all like thorns thrust away, for they cannot be taken with the hand;
and the man who touches them must be armed with iron and a spear’s wood, and they are utterly burned with fire in their place.”{d}

These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite,{e} chief of the three.{f} He was Adino the Eznite; he wielded his spear{g} against eight hundred whom he slew at one time.
And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, son of Ahohi, one of the three mighty men with David when they taunted the Philistines who were gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel went up.
He arose and struck the Philistines until his hand was weary and his hand clung to the sword. And Yahweh wrought a great salvation that day. And the people returned after him only to strip the slain.
And next to him was Shammah son of Agee, a Hararite. When the Philistines had assembled at Lehi,{h} there was a portion of a field full of lentils there, and the people fled before the Philistines.
But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and struck the Philistines. And Yahweh wrought a great salvation.
And three of the thirty chief men went down and came at harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, while a troop of Philistines was encamped in the valley of Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.
And David longed and said, “Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!”

Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water from the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and carried it and brought it to David. But he would not drink it; he poured it out to Yahweh

and said, “Far be it from me, O Yahweh, that I should do this. Is it not the blood of the men who went with their lives in their hands?” So he was not willing to drink it. These things the three mighty men did.
Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three.{i} And he wielded his spear against three hundred and slew them, and he had a name among the three.
Was he not the most honored of the three?{j} And he became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.

And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was the son of a valiant man{k} of Kabzeel, great in deeds. He struck down the two sons of Ariel{l} of Moab. He also went down and struck a lion in the midst of a pit on a day of snow.

And he struck an Egyptian, a man of striking appearance.{m} The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but he went down to him with a club and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear.
These things Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did, and he had a name among the three mighty men.
Among the thirty he was honored, yet to the three he did not come. And David appointed him over his bodyguard.{n}
Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
Shammah of Harod, Elika of Harod,
Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa,
Abiezer of Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah,
Heleb the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the sons of Benjamin,
Benaiah of Pirathon, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash,
Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth of Bahurim,
Eliahba of Shaalbon, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,{o}
Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite,
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite; Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,
Hezro of Carmel, Paarai the Arbite,
Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, who bore the armor of Joab son of Zeruiah,
Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.{p}

notes.text: Or “the favorite of the songs of Israel,” or “the delight of the Strong One of Israel” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “and beautiful are the psalms of Israel” (Brenton, modernized).
Or as a statement: “For he will cause to sprout all my salvation and all my desire.”
Hebrew “belial.”
Hebrew “in the sitting” (uncertain); perhaps “on the spot.”

Josheb-basshebeth means “one who sits in the seat” (uncertain). First Chronicles 11:11 reads “Jashobeam, a Hachmonite”; the Septuagint reads “Jebosthe the Chananite” (Brenton), which may reflect Ishbosheth or Ishbaal (compare 2:8). Marked for scholarly review.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “the captain” or “of the third ones.” Some Septuagint manuscripts reportedly read “of the three.”

So 1 Chronicles 11:11 and the Septuagint (Brenton, “he drew his sword against eight hundred”), in part. The Hebrew phrase “He was Adino the Eznite” is uncertain; Chronicles has instead “he wielded his spear,” and reads “three hundred.” Marked for scholarly review.
Or “at Lehi” (compare Judges 15:9); possibly “in a troop.” Lehi means “jawbone.”
So the Hebrew; two Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac reportedly read “of the thirty.”
Or “He was more honored than the three” (uncertain); compare 1 Chronicles 11:21.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “a living man.”
Ariel perhaps means “lion of God” (uncertain); the Hebrew reads only “the two Ariel of Moab,” perhaps “two champions of Moab.” The Septuagint reads “the two sons of Ariel of Moab” (Brenton).
Hebrew “a man of appearance”; 1 Chronicles 11:23 reads “a man of great stature, five cubits tall” (about 7 feet 6 inches, 2.3 meters).
Hebrew “his bodyguard,” literally “those who listen”; perhaps a privy council.
Hebrew uncertain; 1 Chronicles 11:34 reads “the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shagee.”
The list as it stands names fewer than thirty-seven; the total probably includes the leaders named in verses 8–23 and Joab (uncertain).

verses.text: Once more the anger of Yahweh was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, “Go, number Israel and Judah.”{a}

So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, “Go now to and fro through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and muster the people, that I may know the number of the people.”

But Joab said to the king, “Now may Yahweh your God increase the people a hundredfold, however many they may be, and may the eyes of my lord the king behold it! But my lord the king, why does he take pleasure in this matter?”
Nevertheless the word of the king was stronger than Joab and the army’s commanders. So Joab went out, with the army’s commanders, from before the king to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and encamped at Aroer, on the right side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and on toward Jazer.
Then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi,{b} and they came to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon,
and came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites, and they went out to the Negeb of Judah at Beersheba.
So when they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
And Joab handed over the total of the census of the people to the king: Israel had eight hundred thousand men of valor drawing the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men.{c}

But David’s heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to Yahweh, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O Yahweh, take away, I pray, the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”
And when David arose in the morning, the word of Yahweh came to the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
“Go and say to David, ‘Thus says Yahweh: Three things I lay before you. Choose one of them for yourself, that I may do it to you.’”

So Gad came to David and told him and said to him, “Shall seven{d} years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days’ pestilence in your land? Now consider and see what answer I shall return to him who sent me.”
Then David said to Gad, “I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of Yahweh, for his mercies are great; but let me not fall into the hand of man.”
So Yahweh sent a plague upon Israel from morning to the time appointed.{e} And from Dan even to Beersheba seventy thousand men of the people died.

And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, Yahweh relented from the evil and said to the destroying angel among the people, “Enough! Now let your hand drop.” And the angel of Yahweh was by the threshing floor of Araunah{f} the Jebusite.

Then David spoke to Yahweh when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, “Look, it is I who have sinned, and I who have done wrong. But these sheep, what have they done? Let your hand turn, I beg you, upon me and upon the house of my father.”
And Gad came that day to David and said to him, “Go up, raise an altar to Yahweh on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
So David went up according to the word of Gad, as Yahweh had commanded.
And when Araunah looked down, he saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. And Araunah went out and bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground.
And Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said, “To buy the threshing floor from you, to build an altar to Yahweh, that the plague may be held back from the people.”
Then Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take and offer up what is good in his eyes. Look, the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood.
The whole of it, O king, Araunah hands over to the king.”{g} Araunah said also to the king, “May Yahweh your God take pleasure in you.”

But the king said to Araunah, “No, but I will surely buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for about 20 ounces of silver.{h}
And David built there an altar to Yahweh and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.{i} So Yahweh was moved by entreaty for the land, and the plague was held back from Israel.

notes.text: Compare 1 Chronicles 21:1, where Satan incites David.

Hebrew uncertain; Tahtim-hodshi may mean “lowlands of Hodshi.” The Septuagint reads “the land of Thabason, which is Adasai” (Brenton); some scholars emend to “Kadesh in the land of the Hittites” (reported).
First Chronicles 21:5 gives 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah. The Septuagint here agrees with the Hebrew (Brenton).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint (Brenton) and 1 Chronicles 21:12 read “three.”
Or “until the time of the assembly” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “from morning till noon” and adds that it was the days of wheat harvest (Brenton).

So the traditional reading (qere); the written Hebrew text spells the name in several ways in this chapter (reported). First Chronicles 21:15 calls him Ornan; the Septuagint reads “Orna” (Brenton). The name may be Hurrian, perhaps a title meaning “lord” (uncertain).
Or “All this, O king, does Araunah give to the king.” Some interpreters reportedly read “Araunah the king,” suggesting a former Jebusite ruler.
Hebrew “fifty shekels,” about 20 ounces (575 grams). First Chronicles 21:25 reads “six hundred shekels of gold” (about 15 pounds, 6.9 kilograms) for the whole site.
The Septuagint adds “and Solomon made an addition to the altar afterwards, for it was little at first” (Brenton, modernized).
